idiom_name: sealed token hierarchy + exhaustive when + recursive functions
implementation_notes: Kotlin makes the token side of the structure compile-time checked: a sealed interface (or enum) of token kinds with data classes for payloads, dispatched with an exhaustive when so a new token kind fails compilation until every rule handles it - the mechanism kotlinlang.org documents for sealed hierarchies and when. The parser itself stays ordinary recursive functions over a token list with an index, using when for alternatives, data classes for AST nodes, and exceptions or a result type for errors. What replaces the classic structure is the sealed hierarchy plus exhaustive dispatch: the visitor/switch scaffolding is gone, while one-function-per-rule recursion remains. Use it for the same reasons as any hand-written parser; reach for a generator (ANTLR has a Kotlin target) only when the grammar outgrows hand-written rules.
pitfalls: The JVM stack is fixed and Kotlin has no tail-call optimisation for ordinary functions (tailrec only applies to self-recursive tail calls, which mutually recursive rule functions are not): guard nesting depth explicitly.
Data classes allocate on every token; for hot parsers use value classes or encode kind and offset in an Int/Long instead.
when exhaustiveness is checked against the expression's static type: keep the token list typed as the sealed supertype and never add an else branch, or the guarantee silently disappears.
